💡 Key Takeaways
  • As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.
  • To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia.
  • An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.

To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia. But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components, and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.

An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.

According to recent reports, whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.

The aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.

It has been revealed that few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud organization IONOS as part of a pilot program. It indicates that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a newly introduced class of hardware.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?

Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.

If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a fresh processor that takes care of the heavy math.

Sources indicate that the cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.

Sources indicate that how would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?

In a recent development, light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function. [The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.

Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.

What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?

Industry observers note that the Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.

Linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.

In a recent development, we believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.

What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?

Recent findings suggest that I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.

Under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.

Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?

There’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.

But if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.

Sources indicate that it’s a chicken and egg problem, right? Until developers are building models to run on this type of processor, it’s going to be difficult to sell them to cloud providers. Equally, until photonic processors are available for people to use, it’s going to be tough to convince developers to design for them.

Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology, it will need time to get the credibility and trust that’s needed for a organization like Google to build data center infrastructure around it.

That’s the reason we chose to go into data centers with proof of concept systems, to validate that photonic computing is robust enough to withstand that environment.

We want to invite the world to compute on our systems. We are building a latest chicken, so you can start producing eggs. Let’s find out together whether they’re tasty or not.

What else should I understand about why photonic processors are not already widely in use?

If hypothetically we received an order of 100,000 [photonic processors], we at Q.ANT are ready, but I’m not sure about the suppliers.

Industry observers note that hardware is not software. On the assembly side, it will need [time] before we have the same robust supply chain as the semiconductor world.

Do you expect to suffer from the same problem as other hardware challengers in securing capacity with the big chip manufacturers?

[To produce Q.ANT chips] you only need 90 nanometer node technology, from the 2000s. A lot of foundries already use this capability to produce chips that are super cheap. With this technology, you can use the same line to produce high-performance chips with a much higher street price, without massive upfront investment in your assets.

That resonates well with the industry.

Are Q.ANT processors built to function alongside a particular brand of GPUs—say, Nvidia or AMD—or are they totally agnostic?

There’s no need to go single-sided with a particular GPU. We want to have the freedom to cooperate with any of them.

Either way, we are not competitive to GPUs, we complete their function set.

Can you imagine a future in which AI models run entirely on photonic processors, or will they always be a sidekick?

Recent findings suggest that if we see an opportunity in five years to attack the GPU as well, we would not be shy about taking it. But at the same time, I do not know what workloads in five years are going to be like.

It depends on the architecture of future AI models, you mean?

Could the chance to perform certain calculations more cheaply with photonic processors change the way that AI engineers design future models?

The core message is that we need to do something to fight the energy cost in the AI stack.

That’s where we see the future of AI: very data-optimized models that allow for tasks of the same quality, but at a fraction of the energy—and therefore a fraction of the operating cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was going through a bit of sad time,” Taylor Swift told Jimmy Fallon in 2021 about the lyrics in “All Too Well,” which she cowrote with Liz Rose. “I started ad-libbing what I was going through and what I was feeling.”.

Originally released on Swift’s 2012 album Red, at just under five-and-a-half minutes in length, the song became the focus of her rerecorded Red (Taylor’s Version), after growing into a beloved entry in her catalog among Swifties.

“All Too Well (Taylor’s Version)” rolled out at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 dated Nov. 27, 2021, as Red (Taylor’s Version) opened atop the Billboard 200.

Industry observers note that two versions made the set: one mirroring its original run time and a 10-minute, 13-second take (both of which combined into one listing on Billboard’s charts). They accompanied the 14-minute, 56-second-long All Too Well: The Short Film, directed by Swift and starring Dylan O’Brien, Sadie Sink and Swift.

Given the longer mix of “All Too Well (Taylor’s Version)” (which led its versions in consumption that week), the song became the longest No. 1 in the Hot 100’s history. Don McLean’s “American Pie (Parts I & II),” at 8 minutes and 37 seconds, had held the mark for nearly a half-century.

Plus, with the original “All Too Well” having charted on the Hot 100, at No. 80, for a week in November 2012, Swift notched the first No. 1 cover of a previously charted Hot 100 hit (not counting samples or interpolations) in more than 20 years, since Christina Aguilera, Lil’ Kim, Mya and P!nk’s “Lady Marmalade” in 2001, after the original by Labelle led for a week in March 1975.

Swift additionally became the first artist to send an update of an act’s own prior Hot 100 hit to No. 1 since Elton John, whose “Candle in the Wind 1997″/”Something About the Way You Look Tonight” reigned for 14 weeks in 1997-98. His live version of “Candle” hit No. 6 in 1988, after he had introduced its studio recording in 1973.

In a recent development, in 2022, All Too Well: The Short Film won the Grammy for best music video. Swift also claimed three Moonpersons for it at the MTV Music Video Awards: video of the year, best longform video and best direction.

In a Q&A at Latest York City’s Beacon Theatre during the Tribeca Festival in June 2022, Swift reinforced that the expanded “All Too Well” was a gift to her fans, sharing to applause, “You guys just wouldn’t let it go!”.

#151915. A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1819 w)

A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it.
  • According to recent reports, researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger.
  • It has been revealed that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a fresh lease on life.

According to recent reports, researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

It has been revealed that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

It has been revealed that "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," remarked Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.".

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion.

According to recent reports, for thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Recent findings suggest that once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," stated co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!".

Scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

In a recent development, "When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Latest York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.".

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome.

This kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

In a recent development, as the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

In a recent development, for Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

In a recent development, these surviving systems are crucial because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb.

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

Industry observers note that the telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

The simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao.".

Sources indicate that "It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

According to recent reports, further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De mentioned.

The merger has left astronomers with another vital question: What is Bao like now?

Sources indicate that the surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs.

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.).

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

Earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) showed further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another vital development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

It has been revealed that the telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

Recent findings suggest that scientists quickly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable upcoming measurements.

It has been revealed that webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A Newly introduced Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars.

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an important advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

It has been revealed that that timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

One of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

Industry observers note that the James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel capzized off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities mentioned on Thursday.
  • The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.
  • According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel capzized off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities mentioned on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it capsized about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

According to Spanish authorities, the Med Emre was drifting upside down northwest of Ibiza after capsizing. Initially, they remarked the ship had sunk to the seabed in 1,000 metres of water, but later corrected this statement.

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the incident was not immediately clear.

It has been revealed that the Transport Ministry stated the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency initiative at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government stated it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable.".

But he said the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood.".

Recent findings suggest that "It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he remarked.

According to recent reports, spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

#151911. Industry News: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (789 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen.
  • Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility.
  • Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.

Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times.".

It has been revealed that atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

In a recent development, modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A Newly introduced Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times.

Sources indicate that the researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.".

Sources indicate that that improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A Latest Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity.

Sources indicate that the findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

It has been revealed that for now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

Sources indicate that "Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the significant next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.".

Sources indicate that if successful, such experiments could offer scientists a fresh way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

Materials provided by Kyushu University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#151907. Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (990 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations.
  • The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy.
  • Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

In a recent development, "This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," said Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

It has been revealed that some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

Industry observers note that for lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important, changing how the electrons behave.

One particularly key effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

Sources indicate that "The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang remarked. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

It has been revealed that to test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

According to recent reports, bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

The researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

By measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

It has been revealed that rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

Sources indicate that the findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang said.

Sources indicate that the research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced latest restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.
  • The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced latest restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have unveiled curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it remarked, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

In a recent development, shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based tech giant had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it mentioned last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.

"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.

"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.

Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.

"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.

Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.

While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures.".

Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.

"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.

"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself.".

Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.

Bayern said the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. Discussions between Bayern management and Musiala's representatives are reportedly ongoing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

StudioCanal, the studio unit of Canal+ Group, and Mediatoon Distribution, the content distribution arm of Média-Participations, have struck a European distribution agreement covering three restored animated Asterix film classics.

Industry observers note that the agreement covers three landmark titles from the franchise’s catalogue, namely Asterix the Gaul, Asterix and Cleopatra, and Asterix Conquers Rome, across several European territories, including France, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands. Financial terms weren’t disclosed.

The first major initiative under the partnership will be The Great Asterix Film Festival organized by StudioCanal in Germany from January 2027. “The festival will bring these three films back to the big screen in their restored versions, offering audiences a unique opportunity to rediscover some of the most iconic animated adventures of the famous Gaul,” the manufacturer said on Thursday. “Alongside the theatrical event, a collector’s DVD box set featuring the three films will be released in France and Germany during the 2026 holiday season and in the spring of 2027, respectively. In Poland and the Netherlands, the films will also become available on video-on-demand platforms, reaching new audiences across both territories.”.

Industry observers note that the initiative forms part of a broader effort to celebrate and promote the Asterix universe across Europe. “It will accompany several important milestones in the history of the franchise over the coming years, including the 50th anniversary of Asterix Conquers Rome and the 60th anniversary of Asterix the Gaul in 2028,” StudioCanal noted.

With more than 400 million comic books sold worldwide and generations of readers and viewers captivated over the past six decades, Asterix, created by René Goscinny and Albert Uderzo, is one of Europe’s most successful and enduring cultural franchises. The collaboration also reflects StudioCanal’s long-standing commitment to the Asterix universe, owned by Les Editions Albert René, which holds all exploitation rights.

“Asterix is one of the most iconic works of European popular culture and continues to bring generations together,” stated Pauline Saint-Hilaire, head of catalogue at StudioCanal. “Through this agreement with Mediatoon Distribution, we are delighted to help latest audiences discover, or rediscover, these films in their restored versions and contribute to the lasting appeal of this unique universe.”.

Industry observers note that added Frédéric Gentet, head of sales at Mediatoon Distribution: “For generations, Asterix has brought together audiences of all ages. We are thrilled to join forces with StudioCanal’s to give these animated classics new visibility across Europe. From the Asterix Kino Festival to new digital launches and collector editions, we are celebrating the extraordinary heritage and timeless appeal of one of Europe’s most beloved brands.”.

Breaking: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the earliest moments after the Significant Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma.
  • Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators.
  • One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the earliest moments after the Significant Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal key details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

According to recent reports, however, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory.

According to recent reports, researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

Sources indicate that the researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover latest details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Substantial Bang.

Industry observers note that "Our result reveals a latest source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," claims Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.".

Du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery.

The origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion.".

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

Recent findings suggest that he demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

In a recent development, over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

Recent findings suggest that in conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

"Einstein highlighted that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.".

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma.

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

The team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

In a recent development, they then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

According to recent reports, at first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

Instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

In a recent development, "The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis says. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.".

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid.

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

According to recent reports, even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

Industry observers note that "This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis states. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.".

Industry observers note that the discovery could offer physicists a valuable new tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Big Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

In a recent development, the results also point toward an crucial characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

According to recent reports, du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas.".

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising latest approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover introduced to Mars.
  • The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet.
  • Recent findings suggest that it launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover introduced to Mars.

The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars, or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past.

Recent findings suggest that it launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a newly introduced landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface.

It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet.

Sources indicate that curiosity was the largest rover ever debuted to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success.

According to recent reports, after its smooth landing, Curiosity lived up to its original name: the Mars Science Laboratory. Within weeks, Curiosity fulfilled its primary mission. It found evidence of ancient running water on Mars. It later found organic molecules on Mars as well.

It has been revealed that curiosity's primary mission was expected to last just about one Martian year (687 Earth days, or about two Earth years), as the rover explored its Gale Crater landing site. But NASA has extended the mission as the rover continues to operate in good health.

It has been revealed that in fact, Curiosity has survived long enough to welcome its successor to Mars, the Perseverance rover, which landed in February 2021 on a mission to collect the first samples for later retrieval. Perseverance used the same basic 2-ton design, plutonium power system and sky crane landing system to reach Mars.

And today, a ground-based twin of the Curiosity rover, called Promise, is being outfitted for an upcoming mission to the moon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After the crime dramas “Paatal Lok” on Prime Video and “Kohrra” on Netflix, creator Sudip Sharma is changing lanes with “Pushpak Vimaan,” a black comedy and crime caper starring Jaideep Ahlawat, Abhishek Banerjee and Barun Sobti that is expected on Netflix in early 2027.
  • Two episodes of the series screened at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, after which Sharma, Sobti and Banerjee spoke with Variety.
  • It has been revealed that “I was just feeling the need to change my lane,” Sharma says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After the crime dramas “Paatal Lok” on Prime Video and “Kohrra” on Netflix, creator Sudip Sharma is changing lanes with “Pushpak Vimaan,” a black comedy and crime caper starring Jaideep Ahlawat, Abhishek Banerjee and Barun Sobti that is expected on Netflix in early 2027.

Two episodes of the series screened at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, after which Sharma, Sobti and Banerjee spoke with Variety. Related Stories Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event.

It has been revealed that “I was just feeling the need to change my lane,” Sharma says. The streaming business, he adds, can keep creators returning to successful shows and their sequels. “Honestly, it wasn’t the initiative to be doing only grand dramas. But that’s how life panned out, which is fine. I had real fun doing it. But it felt like I needed to change,” he says. After co-directing the second season of “Kohrra,” he says, “I wanted to just give myself more and newer challenges.”.

“I’m a huge fan of the Coen brothers. Black comedy is my favorite comedy genre,” notes Sharma, who has long been drawn to crime capers. What he wanted to leave behind was the violence. “It was a very deliberate choice. Because I’ve dealt with a lot of violence,” he says. Rather than build the series around a conventional whodunit, he wanted to introduce the characters and their motivations early and let the audience follow the consequences of their choices.

Since he was taking on a genre for the first time, Sharma states, he knew he wanted to be surrounded by friends and brothers. “I wanted people who would have my back, and I would have their backs, and just that feeling of trust,” he says.

Industry observers note that ahlawat starred in “Paatal Lok,” as did Banerjee, who played the hammer-wielding killer Hathoda Tyagi and is now Bhaskar, a startup entrepreneur. Sobti, who worked with Sharma on “Kohrra,” plays Bhupi. “I knew I was writing the part for Jaideep, I knew I was writing the part for Barun,” Sharma says.

When Sobti asked how to approach Bhupi, “‘Just be yourself,’ he told me,” Sobti claims. Sharma describes Sobti as “this really awkward, sweet, kind of confused guy,” not unlike Bhupi. “The quality of writing that he pulls off is remarkable and he’s terrific with his casting,” Sobti says of Sharma. “I really hope this show does well for him.”.

“Finally, someone thinks I’m not just a small-town boy who can play quirky or funny parts, or someone who can only play dark, psychotic characters. I was tired of that,” Banerjee says of the role. Sharma wanted him to play the entrepreneur straight rather than join the comic antics, and Banerjee says situational comedy is his favorite because it is about reacting to the other actors, not playing for laughs.

Sharma describes the Pushpak Vimaan, the flying chariot of the Hindu epic the “Ramayana,” as “that mythical vehicle that can take us from the mess that we are into a place that we want to be in.” His characters, he says, are “all wanting to get away from the morass that they think their life is in, and going for this pot of gold.”.

#151896. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • In a recent development, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

In a recent development, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

Recent findings suggest that "A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," states LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

Sources indicate that to investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Industry observers note that even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred indicates. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

It has been revealed that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

In a recent development, by studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The latest findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

Sources indicate that the research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

Sources indicate that materials provided by California Institute of Technology. Original written by Whitney Clavin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

  • According to recent reports, he should know.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough.".

According to recent reports, he should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.

Akerson noted Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.

In a recent development, "It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a significant change.".

Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable.".

His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, remarked selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.

Sources indicate that "Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.

The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.

Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.

Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.

A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.

Sources indicate that GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the firm's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.

That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates.".

When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.

Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.

Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.

Recent findings suggest that "Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson remarked. "She's done a terrific job.".

Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.

Akerson remarked he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.

"This is key. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
