“I’m always happy when I open that check and deposit it,” Bure added.

In a recent development, the actress played D.J. Tanner, the eldest sister to Stephanie (Jodie Sweetin) and Michelle (Mary-Kate/Ashley Olsen), throughout the show’s run. She also reprised her role in the sitcom’s spin-off Fuller House, which ran for five seasons from 2016 to 2020.

Host Josh McBride also brought up Sweetin’s appearance on the podcast in April 2026, where she shared that her residuals aren’t as great as they used to be.

“I got a one-cent check the other day. No, there’s no syndication anymore because it’s all in streaming. Who gets paid for that? Nobody gets paid for that,” Sweetin stated at the time. “Sure, in my 20s, there would be money, but not reliable. You don’t know how much it’s going to be or how often they’re going to run the show. So, sometimes you’re like, ‘Oh, cool. That was nice.’ And then sometimes you’re like, ‘All right, well, there’s a nice dinner out.'”.

It has been revealed that in response, Bure told McBride, “I actually saw that and she mentioned she doesn’t get much now. And I was like, ‘Jodie, you gotta check with your agent or you gotta call your bank,’ ’cause I still get residuals.”.

Elsewhere on the podcast, Bure also addressed the Olsen twins’ decision not to appear on the spin-off. “It was a bummer because it would have been fun to have everybody back,” she stated of Fuller House. “But at the same time, it wasn’t surprising just because none of us really have stayed close with the girls.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Not because anything went wrong or there was any bad blood. I just think they were kids. They were [filming from] 9 months old until they were 8 years old. They have very different memories than we do. Even me being 10 years older than them, I have significant, great, wonderful memories,” she continued. “They were babies. They probably don’t even remember half the stuff [we do]. They didn’t have the attachment to the crew and the people like we did being older. And they had such a successful fashion business. They haven’t been actors for a long time. They just haven’t been in that part of entertainment.”.

Industry observers note that U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham‘s office has spoken out against an upcoming Channel 4 documentary featuring an interview with disgraced former BBC presenter Huw Edwards.

Industry observers note that announced on Thursday, the doc sees Edwards — who, in 2024, was convicted of three counts of making indecent images of children and given a six-month suspended sentence — speak publicly about his downfall and criminal actions for the first time. Titled “Huw Edwards — Guilty,” it’s set to air on Channel 4 Dec. 1. Related Stories Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event Beyoncé Makes Grammys History as First Artist With 100 Nominations.

The doc has stirred up quite a bit of backlash in the U.K., with several members of Parliament speaking out against it, and now Burnham has added his voice to the mix. In a statement to BBC News, an official spokesperson stated: “Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say.”.

The spokesperson added that these “are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions” and noted that broadcasters “are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions.”.

Asked if the prime minister believed Channel 4 has not acted responsibly by making the documentary, the spokesperson said: “Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them.”.

Sources indicate that representatives for Channel 4 did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment. The broadcaster told the BBC yesterday that the documentary’s director, Patrick Forbes, is “highly experienced” and there were “no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall.”.

#151848. Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Major Bang.
  • Sources indicate that an international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history.
  • Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Major Bang. Each is powered by an enormous black hole that somehow grew to an astonishing size when the Universe was still in its infancy. Scientists have no definitive explanation for how these two cosmic giants became so massive so promptly. The remarkable pair has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

Sources indicate that an international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history. Officially designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the early period known as cosmic dawn.

Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult. Discovering two so close together, especially from such an early period in the Universe's history, makes this finding particularly remarkable.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery was made possible by combining observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawai'i. The research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Gemini North is one of the two telescopes that make up the International Gemini Observatory. Operated by NSF NOIRLab, the observatory is an international partnership led by the U.S. National Science Foundation, with participation from Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea.

How Giant Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe.

During the first billion years after the Significant Bang, the Universe underwent a period of extraordinary transformation. Vast concentrations of invisible matter, known as dark matter halos, collapsed under gravity. The earliest galaxies began producing stars, while increasingly massive galaxies developed the first supermassive black holes at their centers.

As galaxies passed near one another, collided, and sometimes merged, enormous quantities of gas and stars became available to feed their central black holes. Some of the material falling toward these black holes released tremendous amounts of energy. This process, known as accretion, could generate radiation so intense that the glowing region surrounding a black hole outshone every star in its host galaxy.

Astronomers call these extraordinarily luminous objects quasars.

Because galaxy encounters and mergers occur frequently throughout the Universe, researchers expect many quasars to exist in pairs separated by distances smaller than the typical diameter of a galaxy. Yet detecting these systems has remained a major challenge.

According to recent reports, one reason is that a supermassive black hole spends only a relatively brief period in its bright "quasar phase." Another is the enormous distance separating ancient quasars from Earth, which makes them appear extremely faint to ground-based telescopes. Even when both objects are visible, their close proximity can make it difficult to distinguish one from the other.

Two Monster Black Holes That Grew Too Substantial, Too Fast.

Sources indicate that nāpōwawāʻenakaulua stands out because it is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn. More importantly, its two black holes were already so enormous at such an early stage of cosmic history that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth.

According to recent reports, the black holes are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, equivalent to about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. One has an estimated mass of 1.5 billion Suns, while the other weighs approximately 400 million solar masses.

In a recent development, astronomers see the pair as it appeared only 900 million years after the Massive Bang, when the Universe was still populated by relatively young stars, galaxies, and black holes. Finding two black holes comparable in mass to many present-day supermassive black holes at this early time raises difficult questions about how promptly the first enormous cosmic structures could assemble.

Recent findings suggest that "There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two," says Onorato. "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.".

The pair's Hawaiian name reflects the extraordinary forces involved. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua translates to "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.".

The name was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai'i's Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).[1].

How James Webb and Gemini North Revealed the Hidden Pair.

The discovery began with data collected by the Aether survey, a JWST research program designed to identify and characterize objects from the early Universe. The project is led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, an Associate Scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini.

Using JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit, the survey assembled observations of 200 quasars. That sample represents approximately 43% of all quasars known from this period of cosmic history.

While visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed something unexpected. A previously identified quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion.

To investigate, the team turned to Gemini North's Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS). These observations allowed astronomers to distinguish the two quasars individually, providing crucial evidence about the nature of the system.

Obtaining those measurements was an exceptional achievement. The objects are separated by such a small apparent distance, and the companion J1602+4228B is so faint, that resolving them with a telescope on Earth was expected to be nearly impossible.

It has been revealed that fortunately, the researchers benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea. Clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions enabled them to gather the necessary observations in just two nights.

"The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights," claims Onorato.

The team also used Gemini North's Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional information about the system and refine their understanding of the two quasars.[2].

A New Clue to the Universe's First Giant Galaxies.

In a recent development, exactly how Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua formed remains unknown. However, the researchers believe its extraordinary properties could point to an unusually dense concentration of matter in the early Universe.

In such an environment, frequent interactions between young galaxies may have provided enormous supplies of gas, simultaneously accelerating the birth of stars and fueling rapid growth of the black holes at their centers.

If this interpretation is correct, the quasar pair could help scientists understand how the earliest massive galaxies developed alongside their central supermassive black holes.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," states Onorato. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A game Justin Timberlake gave a welcome reminder of his varied talents on The Tonight Show on Thursday night, variously dressing up as a “sexy” turkey, doing a spirited Scottish accent and of course dancing and singing like only he can.

Industry observers note that in what felt like a throwback to the innocence and goofiness of the Obama years, Timberlake was on top form, taking part in sketches, dance bits and sitting down for an interview to promote the 20th anniversary of his classic album FutureSex/LoveSounds and the four-part documentary series Timberlake that begins streaming on Apple TV on Dec. 11. Related Stories TV Justin Timberlake Documentary Trailer: "He's Not Who I Thought He Was" Music Justin Timberlake Teases New Music: "I've Been Chef-ing".

With the Roots backing them up, Fallon opened the show with Timberlake for a song and dance number, with the duo going through The History of Party Songs. In a segment that is catnip for 90s kids, the tracks covered included Soul II Soul’s “Back to Life (However Do You Want Me),” Ini Kamoze’s “Here Comes the Hotstepper,” Mark Morrison’s “Return of the Mack,” Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” Spice Girls “Wannabe,” Bell Biv DeVoe’s “Poison,” Timberlake’s own “Rock Your Body” and more.

In a recent development, in the interview section, Timberlake opened up about the making of FutureSex/LoveSounds, reminding the audience that that his influences on the album included “Bowie, David Byrne, Talking Heads, Freddie Mercury, Queen, Billy Idol, James Brown, Eurythmics and INXS.” He said that on the song “SexyBack” he was channeling Bowie doing “Rebel Rebel” and he had to fight the recording company on the production. “They fought me on it. Well, I brought it in and it was like, ‘It’s too fast.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.’ … [And they said], ‘You don’t sound like you, your signature falsetto.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.'”.

According to recent reports, on the infamous lyrics to “SexyBack”, Timberlake added, “That song does not make any sense. I’ve noted this. It makes zero sense. But, it’s why it makes sense.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a particularly poignant part of the interview, Timberlake discussed his love for and influence of the late D’Angelo, describing him as “my guy.” “D’Angelo, for me, he changed everything. You know, he was one of those artists… rest in peace. What a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant artist. But I remember when he came out, it just like everything changed. [He] was a once-in-a-generation artist.”.

On why he decided to take part in the Apple docuseries — which Fallon said tackled Timberlake’s career highpoints and personal low points — the Grammy-winner said that initially he “was really reluctant to do it” agreeing with Fallon that he was “sort of famously private.” His relationship with director Fisher Stevens softened his stance and that the doc he has “mustered up some courage to talk about some things that I’ve never talked about before, that, you know, things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.”.

In a recent development, timberlake noted he found the doc experience “cathartic” and he hoped it would help others to share their troubles. “Everybody’s going through something. And I think I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that I feel like have made me a better human and a better father, a better husband, a better friend.”.

According to recent reports, in the recent past, Timberlake has had a number of public incidents including being arrested for DWI in the Hamptons in June 2024 and revealing in July 2025 that he was diagnosed with Lyme disease. There was also the cheating rumors in 2019, and subsequent public ridicule, after the singer was caught holding hands with co-star Alisha Wainwright during the filming of Palmer. Timberlake had to concern a public apology about the Palmer incident on Instagram, calling it a “strong lapse in judgment.”.

Industry observers note that one sketch that’s likely to get a lot of play on social media was “Sexy Butterball Hotline,” where Fallon (Rocky Drumstick) and Timberlake (Pecker Spatchcock) played two very sexy turkeys — “the dirtiest birds in the coop” no less — manning an after dark Thanksgiving helpline. A sample of some of the lines from Rocky and Pecker in this bit: “Who indicates the turkey can’t be the one who does the stuffing?” “Is it Black Friday? ‘Cause my clothes are 100% off.” “I can’t wait till you lay me down on the table right in front of Grandma.” Good clean fun.

It wouldn’t be a complete Timberlake Tonight Show appearance without a “Camp Winnipesaukee” sketch. Fallon and Timberlake once more donned the retainers and wigs to relive their awkward teenage years and play the annoying campers trying to sing a popular song much to the annoyance of the camp counselor. On Thursday’s episode, the pair decided to take on The Proclaimers’ 1988 hit “I’m Gonna Be (500 Miles)” with Timberlake and Fallon’s attempt at Scottish brogue worthy of commendation but ultimately short of passable.

Recent findings suggest that proving he’s still one of the greatest singers and dancers around, Timberlake rounded his appearance with two medleys of his greatest hits. In the first clip he performed a medley of “FutureSex / LoveSound,” “SexyBack,” “Summer Love” and “My Love.”.

In a second clip he performed “LoveStoned,” “Until the End of Time” and “What Goes Around…/ … Comes Around.”.

On farewell trip, Steinmeier calls for more investment in Africa

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was notable to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," mentioned Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa.
  • "For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana.
  • This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was notable to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," mentioned Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa. Over the course of 20 years, as president and before that as foreign minister, the veteran politician has made 30 trips to African countries.

"For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana. He was alluding to the first German-African business summit in Berlin in 2015, which Steinmeier opened while he was still foreign minister in the administration of former Chancellor Angela Merkel.

This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.

A lot has happened since 2015, Steinmeier said. And yet: "We are still far from where we could be." Addressing Germany's business community, he said, "Be curious, take risks.".

Industry observers note that as the applause rang out after the speech, Jude Numfor, who works for the energy firm REI in Cameroon, smiled. He too sees German companies as too risk-averse.

"When the Chinese come, they say 'let's do it,' and the Germans say 'let's prepare it'," he told DW.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Africa's economy is growing rapidly. German-African foreign trade rose by 10.5% in 2025 to €63.4 billion ($69.4 billion). Africa's trade with the Asia-Pacific region is growing more slowly, but the absolute figures are also significantly higher.

This demonstrates there is a great deal of potential in Africa's markets — especially in light of the emerging African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which encompasses most of the continent.

When it comes to direct investment, German companies are more hesitant than others — a trend observed not only by Numfor: China, Turkey and the Gulf states are willing to take on more risk and are pushing into these markets.

In a recent development, the Chinese, in particular, are offering large loans to build key rail lines and ports, and they are buying up mines and raw materials in Africa. But since they usually bring their own low-wage labor force with them, China's investments often create few local jobs.

Sources indicate that but such jobs would be the linchpin of Africa's future. In Kenya alone, 1 million young people enter the labor market each year; in Nigeria, the number is even higher, and some experts therefore anticipate even more irregular migration to Europe in the coming years.

Germany has said there is a need for action: It supports vocational training in Africa and, for several years now, has also been allowing skilled workers to emigrate to Germany from Africa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that during his trip, Steinmeier also visited educational institutions such as the vocational school for mechanics and industrial maintenance in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire. In Kenya, he spoke with President William Ruto about the implications of the 2024 bilateral migration and mobility partnership and more opportunities for language and vocational training.

It has been revealed that there are now around 9,500 Kenyans working in Germany, and nearly 1,300 in vocational training. "We want to open up opportunities for young people and create regular, fair and orderly pathways for labor and skilled worker migration," Steinmeier noted in Nairobi.

Vocational training is stated to be most effective where businesses and factories are being established.

"A very favorable window of opportunity for investment is currently opening up in Africa," remarked Fritz Audebert, CEO of ICUnet, a organization that advises German firms on investment projects worldwide. "We've noticed a shift over the past two years or so, driven in part by geopolitical changes, the complicated situation in China, and most recently the war in Iran.".

"More and more companies are beginning to understand this," Audebert added. "While there are reservations, we're seeing a similar sentiment to that regarding India." What's latest is that small and medium-sized enterprises from Germany are also showing interest in Africa.

It has been revealed that during the trip, Audebert was particularly impressed by Cote d'Ivoire, as he said, "because of the ministers' high level of expertise." The country is the world's largest cocoa exporter and possesses notable raw materials. "You can work well with this potential," he said.

Members of the business delegation accompanying Steinmeier also agreed that the German automotive industry must focus more on the African market.

"The middle class is growing in cities, and with it, the demand for mobility," remarked Audebert.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Markus Thill, president of Bosch Africa, confirms there is a considerable market for simple, gas- and diesel-driven cars. "Based on the auto industry's experience, we know that households worldwide with an annual income of €10,000 or more can afford a upcoming car," remarked Thill. This would mean that potentially 5-10 million new cars per year could be built and sold in Africa.

Instead, "we export millions of old used cars to Africa that would no longer be eligible for registration in Europe," he said.

In a recent development, even though the focus of the trip was on the economy, "we shouldn't limit our view to that," Steinmeier remarked at the end of his trip. Germany maintains a reliable political partnership with Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana and Kenya.

"These are three countries with which we cooperate closely on the international stage, and in that sense, visiting them now was the right and deliberate choice," he noted.

When asked to take stock of his 30 trips to African countries undertaken during his political career, Steinmeier said: "There is not one Africa, but many, and there are also very different, uneven developments there." This fact, he concluded, needs to be "communicated even more effectively" in Germany.

This article was originally written in German.

It has been revealed that tyson Fury does not have schizophrenia, despite revelations made in the promo for his newly introduced Netflix feature doc. These revelations have now been removed from the film.

In the trailer for “Tyson Fury,” the British boxing champion is seen discussing his mental health struggles, noting that when quizzed by a psychiatrist he “ticked all the boxes … depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder…” Fury’s wife then adds that he’s a “mild schizophrenic.” Related Stories Rosalía, Hilary Duff, and Slayyyter to Be Honored at Variety’s Hitmakers Event Beyoncé Makes Grammys History as First Artist With 100 Nominations.

Industry observers note that the comments sparked numerous headlines and also prompted British boxing regulators to look into the matter to ensure that Tyson would be medically cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in their long-awaited bout due to take place Dec. 11. But now Paris Fury has walked back those claims, putting out a statement denying that her husband has schizophrenia. Netflix has subsequently edited the scene in question out of the documentary.

It has been revealed that “I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” Paris Fury remarked. “I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic’. While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.”.

Added a Netflix spokesperson: “Following fresh information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch.”.

Now showing on Netflix and directed by Lucy Wilcox, “Tyson Fury” charts the triumphs and setbacks of the heavyweight champion’s career, his struggles with mental health and addiction, the loss of a child, complex family relationships and the question of what it means to be a man.

The film was produced by Optomen, part of Banijay Entertainment, which also produced Netflix’s “At Home With the Furys” reality show featuring the boxer and his family, now onto its third season.

#151842. This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a significant impression on scientists.
  • Industry observers note that the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes.
  • It has been revealed that many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a significant impression on scientists. Although it is only about the size of a quarter, the spider has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome.

Industry observers note that the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes. Its unusually large genome seems particularly fitting given Colbert's famously pompous television persona on the former Comedy Central show "The Colbert Report.".

It has been revealed that many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween. But this particular spider stands out for something that cannot be seen with the naked eye: the extraordinary amount of DNA packed into its tiny body.

"At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant," said corresponding author Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology.

In a recent development, according to Bond, this is the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a spider belonging to this family. The findings were published in the Journal of Heredity.

A Secretive Spider That Hunts From Underground.

Visitors to the coastal dunes of Northern California may unknowingly pass close to these spiders without ever spotting one. Most of their lives unfold beneath the sand, where they remain hidden in carefully constructed burrows.

According to recent reports, female trapdoor spiders spend their entire lives underground in tunnels lined with silk. Each burrow has a hinged entrance that blends into its surroundings, allowing the spider to stay concealed while monitoring activity outside.

In a recent development, when an unsuspecting insect or other prey animal approaches, vibrations alert the spider to its presence. At precisely the right moment, the spider bursts through its hidden door to capture its next meal.

Although these spiders are skilled ambush predators, their venom poses no danger to humans. Bond noted that among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

A Spider Genome Bigger Than the Human Genome.

The spider's DNA contains more surprises than its sheer size. Researchers found that its genome includes 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human cells, which are organized into 23 pairs.

According to recent reports, however, having a larger genome does not necessarily mean having more genes. In this spider, approximately 77% of the genome consists of repetitive DNA sequences that appear many times throughout its genetic material.

Sources indicate that the research also highlights an unusual feature of spider chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional repetitive DNA sequences associated with telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. This difference could help explain why spider chromosomes appear to evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

"It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life," Bond said.

Why Is the Spider Named After Stephen Colbert?

The story behind the spider's unusual scientific name dates back to 2008, when Stephen Colbert discovered that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young.

Recent findings suggest that not wanting to be left out, Colbert turned the situation into a comedy segment. During "Who's Not Honoring Me Now?" on "The Colbert Report," he publicly demanded that Bond name a spider in his honor.

Bond agreed, and Aptostichus stephencolberti became Colbert's namesake in the spider world.

Rising Seas Threaten California's Trapdoor Spiders.

Beyond revealing the spider's genetic peculiarities, the research could play an crucial role in protecting the species.

The genome sequencing effort is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative designed to build a collection of genomic information that scientists can use to guide conservation decisions.

Recent findings suggest that trapdoor spiders generally do not venture far from their burrows, making it difficult for populations to move between habitats. Because their coastal dune environments are already separated into isolated areas, researchers hope genetic information will help them identify distinct populations that may need special protection.

"We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us," Bond mentioned. "We're hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.".

Aptostichus stephencolberti (the "t" in Colbert is silent) is found only in coastal dunes along a limited stretch of Central California, extending from the San Francisco Bay area to Monterey.

Recent findings suggest that this restricted range makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels could eliminate portions of its coastal habitat, while invasive species pose another significant danger.

"They're going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they're also very sensitive to invasive species," Bond said.

Spider Venom Could Hold Clues to Latest Medicines.

Recent findings suggest that the potential benefits of studying this spider's genome extend beyond conservation and evolutionary biology. Scientists also hope that understanding spider genetics will help them explore the vast range of chemical compounds found in spider venom.

Some substances identified in spider venoms have shown promise as potential painkillers, while others could be useful in developing new ways to control agricultural pests.

With so many spider species still poorly understood at the genetic level, researchers believe their venoms may contain valuable compounds that have yet to be discovered.

"We don't really know what's out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms," Bond mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that the study's additional authors include Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe and Oanh Nguyen of UC Davis; Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann and Merly Escalona of UC Santa Cruz; Robert D. Cooper of Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University; and H. Bradley Shaffer and Erin Toffelmier of UCLA.

The research received support from the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California through the state of California's State Budget Act of 2019, as well as from the National Science Foundation.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

According to recent reports, U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

In a recent development, many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

Industry observers note that it's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," mentioned Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt remarked.

Sources indicate that "People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites.".

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

Sources indicate that its fresh cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.).

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 right now to somewhere in the 30s.

Sources indicate that "You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, noted in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats.".

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

Industry observers note that and there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American remarked. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

According to recent reports, "It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt noted. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer.".

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

In a recent development, american will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each confirmed their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

Sources indicate that there are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline states.

"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done.".

It has been revealed that although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month remarked it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter noted last month.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that british actor Arthur Conti is fresh off a whirlwind year.
  • “To play an iconic character that’s been played by many people before, and to get to give your own spin on it, is very exciting,” Conti tells The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom from London about what he’s been up to this year.
  • The 22-year-old actor is back in the U.K.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that british actor Arthur Conti is fresh off a whirlwind year. With roles in Mike Flanagan’s Carrie adaptation and the recently released Ebenezer, he’s been busy crafting newly introduced interpretations of well-known characters.

“To play an iconic character that’s been played by many people before, and to get to give your own spin on it, is very exciting,” Conti tells The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom from London about what he’s been up to this year.

The 22-year-old actor is back in the U.K. after over a month of press for Carrie and Ebenezer and a stint in Portland, Oregon. “It’s been a bit of a whirlwind, but it’s been very enjoyable,” he says. After a breakout performance in 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, 2026 has been the actor’s biggest year to date between the two projects and a role in Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Related Stories TV Why Mike Flanagan Just Couldn't Kill Carrie White Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up.

According to recent reports, with Carrie, Conti stepped into the role of teen bully Billy Nolan, first played on screen by John Travolta in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. Conti had read Stephen King’s novel but hadn’t seen De Palma’s film, which he stayed away from during filming. Conti’s Billy, while still one of the villains of the story, is different from Travolta’s take on the character. “I was worried that even inadvertently or subconsciously I would copy things about that performance, and I really wanted it to be all my own,” he notes.

Ebenezer finds Conti stepping into the shoes of the titular character of Ebenezer Scrooge — well, the younger version of him anyway. The actor heard that Ti West would be making the film, and as a major fan, he sent in a self-tape. Much like with Carrie, he tried not to take too much inspiration from previous versions of the story, but there’s one adaptation that stands out.

In a recent development, “[The Muppets version] is probably the best one. I mean, it’s amazing, that film. Michael Caine gives such a genuinely brilliant, dramatic performance in that film against the Muppets,” he notes. “He takes it so seriously, and that is the beauty of that film is that you’d think he was talking to John Gielgud, and he’s talking to Fozzy.”.

In a recent development, despite The Muppets Christmas Carol being his main experience with the story beforehand, he did watch the 1951 film adaptation starring Alastair Sim as Scrooge. “I really liked,” he notes.

Below, the actor digs into his last year in roles, what he’s looking to do next and how he’d spend a perfect day in London.

I’m always curious, as someone who enjoys it — have you seen Carrie: The Musical?

We watched it. We saw a theater production on Granville Island in Vancouver. It was a youth theater production of Carrie: The Musical. [The cast of Carrie] all went to go and see it. Mike [Flanagan] actually put the cast of that production of Carrie in the show. They’re all at the prom. Throughout the show, they’re in the background at the school, which was really, really fun.

Sources indicate that how has the year been? You were busy with Carrie and now Ebenezer.

[Carrie] was my first big press tour. It was my first time doing a press junket and all of these things. It feels like the biggest thing that I’ve done so far [with] how much I’ve been promoting it. It was all incredibly exciting. [In Carrie,] I’m playing another character that has several sides to him, after [I did in] Beetlejuice. It’s another deceptively charming, manipulative character, which is interesting that I keep taking. (Laughs).

Where do you think that’s coming from?

Something about me, I don’t know. Something untrustworthy. Honestly, it is a treat to play characters like that because you get the chance to do multiple things at once, present a character that has many layers and is complex and isn’t wholly one thing or another. It was a great role. It was a really meaty role to sink my teeth into, and it was an honor to play a character of that literary significance. It was a privilege to be entrusted with that.

As an actor, are you drawn to characters that are different from you, then?

It’s nice to get outside of yourself — that’s part of the fun of it. Growing up, the films I was watching, I was a lot more drawn to flawed or strange or darker characters. I grew up watching Steve Buchemi in Fargo and Philip Seymour Hoffman in Punch-Drunk Love and Talented Mr. Ripley. Those are the kind of characters that I always really loved to watch.

The scope of the projects you had this year has been quite large. Are you drawn to that or looking to change it?

You’re right. They are quite large-scale. I think I’m drawn to things that are a little out there and a little strange. Horror is one of the best genres to explore that area because it emboldens filmmakers to experiment and take risks and be a bit weird and a bit dreamlike. That’s why I gravitate towards horror a lot, and it’s probably what I watch the most of in the cinema.

Is that where you got your love for it? Were you massive into horror as a kid?

Sources indicate that I think so. It’s not horror, just things that are a little strange. My mom brought me up on Charlie Kaufman films. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is my mom’s favorite film, so I watched that quite early. Things that tap into that dreaminess and that weirdness and spookiness — that’s up my alley. But it would be a dream to do a Before Sunrise kind of thing, where it’s just two people talking for an hour and a half. I would love to do something like that next.

Is that what you’re looking to do going forward then?

It has been revealed that it could be anything. I really want to leave myself open. I would love to do something a little more scaled down, kind of dialogue-heavy thing. I could never have imagined the caliber of director and the caliber of actor that I’ve been working with. If I can only just continue to do that, I will be very lucky indeed. I’ve gotten to work with some of my absolute heroes, and that’s been wonderful. But I want to keep working in horror as well. Horror’s having a really exciting moment right now, especially young people in horror, with Obsession and Backrooms. I will stay as long as it’ll have me. Horror, fantasy — that’s what I grew up with, and I want to explore that more as well.

What does your ideal day off look like?

According to recent reports, I would wake up at 10:30 a.m.-ish. I’m a very late-to-bed, late-to-rise kind of person in my free time. I’d wake up then; I’d get a coffee; I’d go for a walk. I have to do 10,000 steps a day. I’m like a dog. I have to be walked. Then I would go and see a movie. I would go to the cinema. I would probably go to the Prince Charles Cinema, which is my favorite in the world. I don’t know whether I’d see it on my own or with somebody else. I do go on my own to the cinema a lot. That’s one of my favorite ways to watch a film. Then I’d get a nice dinner. I might go shopping a little bit. I might go record shopping, go DVD shopping. Then I would go to the pub maybe, and then I would go to bed at 1 a.m. I’m being very specific with the times.

I’m unfamiliar with Prince Charles Cinema; why is that your favorite theater?

It has been revealed that just the vibe there, and the programming. There’s always something on there that’s worth seeing. I honestly have so much to thank that cinema for because the education in film that it has given me is just insane. I’ve seen so many films there for the first time. It’s one of the few places, in London especially, where you can see old films and cult films and things that don’t get screened very often. You can go and experience them in the theater, and that’s a very valuable thing. They were going to possibly get shut down, but they’ve just won the battle against the landlord or whatever. They’re going to be there for another 25 years. I’m very happy about that.

Tech Report: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.
  • Sources indicate that that isn't a random comparison.
  • A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.

Sources indicate that that isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao.

A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER).

According to recent reports, "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University remarked in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events.".

The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy, a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion.

According to recent reports, responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years,.

They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits.

"A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar remarked. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years.".

According to recent reports, an important clue to how this cataclysmic and cannibalistic event proceeded was provided by SPHEREx in July 2025, which found that before the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light but brightening in infrared. This indicated that Big Bao was cooling down and spewing out dense clouds of gas and dust that were enveloping the red giant star.

Recent findings suggest that when Little Bao crashed into the core of Big Bao, it caused stellar material to be ejected at speeds of around 1.8 million miles per hour. This matter crashed into the envelope of gas and dust previously spewed by Big Bao, and this caused the flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025.

One of the final pieces of this story was provided by the JWST on Dec. 24, 2025. The powerful space telescope measured the total mass of dust and gas around Massive Bao prior to the eruption since two months earlier.

This helped determine that Little Bao had a mass of around 70% of the sun's mass.

"It was kind of symbolic how the year was coming to an end as we managed to bring together the puzzle pieces from the story of Significant and Little Bao," Karambelkar stated. "But in my mind, this felt like a closure of just one chapter in a story that is just starting. We learned so much about AT2025abao, but we also learned much about conducting coordinated, multi-facility, multi-team astronomical discoveries.".

Industry observers note that the team's research was published on Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
  • Researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown.
  • Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. For approximately one hour, the star gradually grew brighter before fading back to its usual appearance. The change was smooth and symmetrical, with no sudden explosion or flare. It looked as though an invisible object had moved between Earth and the star, bending its light in our direction. Afterward, the star returned to normal and revealed no further changes in brightness.

Researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown. The event appears to be an example of gravitational microlensing, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. When a compact object with sufficient mass passes in front of a distant star, its gravity bends the star's light and temporarily magnifies its brightness. This produces a recognizable pattern that differs from the changes caused by variable stars, stellar flares, or passing asteroids.

Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The distinctive pattern convinced the team that they had detected a genuine gravitational microlensing event. What remained uncertain was the nature of the invisible object responsible.

Three Possible Explanations for the Mysterious Object.

Researchers have identified three potential explanations for Phoebe. One possibility is a rogue planet that was expelled from its original solar system and now travels alone through the Milky Way. Another is a similar wandering planet located within the Large Magellanic Cloud. If the second explanation proves correct, Phoebe would become the first planet discovered through gravitational microlensing beyond our galaxy.

The third possibility is far more extraordinary. Phoebe could be a primordial black hole, an ancient object that formed in the earliest moments of the universe. Unlike ordinary black holes, which develop when massive stars collapse, primordial black holes could have emerged from extremely dense regions of space during the first fractions of a second after the Major Bang. Such objects would have formed long before the first stars appeared.

A One-Hour Signal Reveals a Surprising Clue.

The unusually short duration of the brightening provides an key clue about Phoebe's mass. Gravitational microlensing events depend partly on how massive the intervening object is. Generally, lighter objects produce shorter events, although their speed and position also influence how long the magnification lasts.

It has been revealed that phoebe's signal lasted approximately 60 minutes, placing it near the detection limit of current astronomical surveys. Using the observed duration and their models of the event, researchers estimated that the object has a mass roughly three times that of the Moon. That would make it considerably less massive than any planet in our solar system and far too small to be a conventional black hole formed by a collapsing star.

Black holes produced through stellar collapse typically have masses of at least about five times that of the Sun. Phoebe's estimated mass falls enormously below that threshold. If the mysterious object really is a black hole, its tiny mass would point toward a primordial origin rather than the death of a star.

Could Phoebe Be a Primordial Black Hole Linked to Dark Matter?

In a recent development, to investigate where Phoebe might belong, the researchers compared the likelihood that the object originated from different populations. These included stars in the Milky Way, stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and objects associated with the surrounding dark matter halo.

The results strongly favored the dark matter halo. According to the team's calculations, Phoebe is approximately 100,000 times more likely to belong to this population than to one associated with ordinary stellar matter. This enormous difference makes a potential connection to dark matter particularly intriguing, although it does not establish that Phoebe is a primordial black hole.

Recent findings suggest that if the primordial black hole interpretation is correct, Phoebe could be among the oldest objects ever detected. It may have formed before the first atoms and stars existed, when the universe was still experiencing the extreme conditions that followed the Major Bang.

For roughly 13 billion years, such an object could have traveled unseen through space, leaving almost no trace of its existence. Then, on a single night in December 2019, its gravity may have briefly magnified the light of a distant star, offering astronomers a remarkable glimpse of something born near the very beginning of the universe.

Scientists Use ‘Grand Theft Auto’ to Model the Effects of Climate Change

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most enticing features of Grand Theft Auto (GTA) is the incredibly well-realized worlds, especially among the most recent installments in the franchise.
  • Sources indicate that developed by Rockstar Games, GTA is one of the most valuable intellectual properties in the video game industry.
  • Like the recently released game—which is so detailed you can even go birding in it—GTA V is a meticulous recreation of the real world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most enticing features of Grand Theft Auto (GTA) is the incredibly well-realized worlds, especially among the most recent installments in the franchise. In this detailed rendering, researchers saw an unusual opportunity: What if these video games could be used to model the effects of the climate crisis?

Sources indicate that developed by Rockstar Games, GTA is one of the most valuable intellectual properties in the video game industry. As of this year, the franchise has sold an estimated 465 million units worldwide, and the latest installment in the series, GTA VI, earned $3.79 billion in first-day sales.

Like the recently released game—which is so detailed you can even go birding in it—GTA V is a meticulous recreation of the real world. It’s setting, Los Santos, is a fictional city inspired by Los Angeles and consists of pretty much the same topographical, urban, and coastal features of the Californian metropolis.

These specs were leveraged by Paul Nörenberg, a professor at the University of Potsdam in Germany, and his colleague Hugues Lantuit of the Alfred Wegener Institute, who conducted an experiment to determine whether the video game could serve as a useful tool for projecting the severity and impact of flooding and sea-level rise under various future scenarios related to global warming.

It has been revealed that the authors of the study, published in Geoscience Communication, created a digital model based on the video game’s three-dimensional terrain maps. This allowed them to estimate which areas of Los Santos would be submerged if sea levels continue to rise.

The researchers calculated these possibilities based on two climate scenarios used in the projections of the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

The first, known as RCP 2.6, assumes that countries implement effective measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and limit global warming. The second, called RCP 8.5, envisions a scenario of high emissions without sufficient mitigation measures. In both cases, the authors made projections of potential climate impacts for the years 2100, 2300, and 2500, and included simulations of storm surges.

In a recent development, the results showed that, in a high-emissions scenario and in the event of a storm surge, sea-level rise and coastal flooding could reach 5.18 meters by 2300. The model estimates that, under these conditions, 5.1 percent of Los Santos’ land area would be flooded, affecting the port, wastewater treatment facilities, and coastal energy infrastructure.

Estimates for the same scenario, but for the year 2500, project that the combined water level would reach 8.22 meters and that 6.5 percent of the land area would be submerged. In contrast, under the emissions-reduction scenario, flooding would affect only 2.2 percent of the territory by 2300, without impacting major infrastructure.

It has been revealed that in a second phase, the researchers sought to verify whether the simulations based on the GTA V map could reflect what would happen in the real city. To do so, they compared the results of their model with scientific data on the areas of Los Angeles most vulnerable to flooding. The comparison revealed that the areas identified as vulnerable in the video game coincided with the three locations in the real city most likely to experience flooding: Venice Beach, Pacific Palisades, and the Port of Los Angeles.

“This congruence supports the conclusion that the GTA V terrain is sufficiently faithful to real-world morphology to be scientifically meaningful,” the authors write. The researchers caution, however, that their results should not be interpreted as an exact prediction, since the GTA V model and maps do not account for all possible real-world phenomena that influence flood risk, including wave motion, beach erosion, currents, or changes in terrain.

Industry observers note that the researchers also see a benefit from using GTA V to model climate effects that extends beyond the results themselves. Not only does Los Santos look like the real world, but millions of people have spent countless hours exploring it. For the connection many have to these games, a climate model based in this simulation might feel closer to reality.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

Recent findings suggest that later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses. Her lawyers caused further delay when they mentioned she would not confirm her personal information.

In a recent development, several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys stated their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.

The Russian ambassador was summoned regarding the incident, and Andrei Mayerov, the deputy military attache at the embassy, was expelled from Germany.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.

Her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws. She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.

She was also noted to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

Sources indicate that on several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.

In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.

Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.

The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.

#151831. Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans.
  • A fresh study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans. Yet scientists are still working to answer a fundamental question about our planet's history: Where did all this carbon originally come from?

A fresh study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer. Researchers have uncovered chemical evidence suggesting that much of Earth's carbon may have arrived aboard ancient meteorites during a particular stage of the planet's formation. Even more remarkably, the findings suggest that some of this carbon became trapped deep inside Earth's core before eventually making its way back to the surface.

Sources indicate that the discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks. Researchers believe these chemical fingerprints may reveal carbon that originated in Earth's core and traveled upward through the planet's interior.

"We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth's core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface," says lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor in Columbia University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How Carbon Could Escape From Earth's Core.

To understand how carbon might travel from Earth's deepest interior to its surface, it helps to look at the planet's internal structure.

In a recent development, beneath Earth's thin outer crust lies the mantle, a vast region of mostly solid rock extending approximately 1,800 miles downward. Below that is the outer core, a roughly 1,400-mile-thick layer of molten metal surrounding the extremely hot, dense, solid metallic inner core.

Scientists believe that most of Earth's carbon is stored in its core. However, directly examining this material is far beyond the reach of current technology, and researchers may never be able to obtain samples from such extreme depths.

Fortunately, Earth's volcanic activity offers another way to investigate what lies below.

It has been revealed that recent studies suggest that certain elements can escape from the outer core and enter the overlying mantle. From there, they may be transported toward the surface by enormous rising columns of hot rock known as mantle plumes.

Sources indicate that these plumes begin near the boundary between the core and mantle. As they ascend, some of the rock partially melts, producing magma that can eventually erupt through volcanoes.

It has been revealed that when that magma cools, crystals begin to grow. Occasionally, these crystals trap tiny droplets of molten material before dissolved gases have a chance to escape. The trapped droplets, known as undegassed melt inclusions, preserve valuable chemical information about the original magma.

"These melts are fossils of the magma," Moussallam notes.

Because magma contains dissolved gases, including carbon dioxide, these microscopic pockets provide scientists with a rare opportunity to study carbon that may have traveled upward from Earth's core.

Hawaiian Volcanoes Reveal an Unusual Carbon Signature.

Hawaii is particularly well suited for this kind of investigation. Previous research has established that its volcanoes receive magma associated with a deep mantle plume, potentially providing access to material originating near the boundary with Earth's core.

Moussallam and his colleagues examined volcanic rocks from eruptions at Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift. Using a recently developed analytical technique, they measured carbon isotopes preserved inside undegassed melt inclusions.

Carbon isotopes are different forms of the same element that have slightly different masses. By comparing their relative abundance, scientists can identify chemical signatures that offer clues about where carbon came from and what processes it experienced.

The Tantalus Rift samples are thought to represent magma originating near the outer margins of the mantle plume. Earlier research established that typical mantle carbon has an isotopic signature between approximately -5 and -7 per mil, a measurement expressing small differences in isotope ratios. The researchers found that the Tantalus Rift samples closely matched this expected range.

The Kīlauea samples, however, told a very different story.

Magma beneath Kīlauea is believed to originate closer to the center of the mantle plume, where material may rise from near the core-mantle boundary. In these samples, the scientists detected carbon with a much heavier isotopic signature of approximately -1 per mil.

This unusual value has rarely been observed before and differs substantially from the signature normally associated with Earth's mantle.

"This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle," says Moussallam. "This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core.".

Recent findings suggest that although the team considers Earth's core the most likely source, Moussallam emphasizes that the evidence is not yet definitive. Additional measurements will be necessary to establish whether the carbon truly originated there.

Ancient Meteorites May Explain Where Earth's Carbon Came From.

The unusual carbon signature also provided researchers with a possible clue about events that occurred more than 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was still forming.

According to Moussallam, the isotopic composition of carbon in Earth's core should preserve "the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created.".

To investigate that possibility, the team compared the distinctive Kīlauea measurements with carbon signatures found in ancient meteorites. They discovered similarities to a group of meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites.

Chondrites are among the oldest known materials in our solar system, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. They preserve clues about the primitive material from which planets formed.

"All of Earth is made of chondrites," Moussallam explains. "They're the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets.".

Scientists generally distinguish between two broad categories of chondrites. Noncarbonaceous chondrites formed in the inner solar system, while carbonaceous chondrites, which contain more carbon, originated in the outer regions of the solar system.

Exactly how much each type contributed to Earth's formation has remained a subject of scientific debate.

The newly introduced findings support the possibility that carbonaceous chondrites made an especially crucial contribution during the later stages of Earth's development.

In a recent development, according to the researchers' proposed explanation, these carbon-rich meteorites struck the growing planet at a time when it had become better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have accumulated deep within Earth, eventually becoming part of the planet's enormous internal carbon reservoir.

Over billions of years, carbon from that reservoir could have migrated upward through mantle plumes and emerged in volcanic eruptions.

If the interpretation is correct, some of the carbon essential to life today may have arrived from the outer solar system aboard meteorites during Earth's earliest history.

A Remarkable Journey From Space to Life on Earth.

Despite the intriguing evidence, vital questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not conclusively demonstrated that the unusual carbon came from Earth's core or established precisely how much of the planet's carbon was delivered by carbonaceous meteorites.

Industry observers note that "We don't really know. We need more measurements," cautions Moussallam.

Nevertheless, the findings offer a fascinating possible connection between the formation of the solar system, the inaccessible depths of our planet, and the carbon that makes life possible.

They also raise the possibility that some of the carbon found in living organisms today has followed an extraordinary path. After arriving on Earth billions of years ago, it may have become incorporated into the planet's metallic core, moved slowly upward through the mantle, and eventually returned to the surface through volcanic eruptions.

Industry observers note that "It's fun to think about. We're made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet's core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting.".

Sources indicate that the study was coauthored by Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, and Bridgett Holman of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory; Damanveer S. Grewal of Yale University; Estelle F. Rose-Koga of Institut des Sciences de la Terre d'Orléans; Allan Lerner of the US Geological Survey; Paul J. Wallace of the University of Oregon; and Natália Gauer.
